name: Pattern 8: Feedback Before Grades
title: Pattern 8: Feedback Before Grades
answer: Feedback Before Grades is a pattern where AI gives students comments on a draft before a teacher grades the final version. The student revises using feedback tied to the class rubric, and the teacher alone assigns the grade. It matters because it can improve revisions and motivation while keeping grading authority with the teacher.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: The pattern solves the problem of feedback arriving too late or too thinly to help students improve. Instead of waiting for a final grade, a student submits a draft, such as an essay, a lab report, a proof, or a block of code, and receives quick comments linked to the class rubric. The student then revises the work. Only after that revision does the teacher read and grade the final version. The AI never produces the grade.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The text does not give separate grade bands for this pattern. It describes the routine for student work in general, and its evidence comes from tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language. In a classroom, the teacher would set the rubric, have students submit a draft, and let AI provide comments tied to that rubric. Students then revise, and the teacher grades the final version. The design shown in Figure 2.6 makes revision part of the assignment and keeps the grade with the teacher.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this pattern as having "some of the best evidence in the Volume." A randomized trial with 459 tenth graders writing in English as a foreign language found that AI feedback improved the quality of revisions and raised motivation compared with revising without feedback (Meyer et al., 2023). A later trial found no clear difference in revision quality between teacher feedback and AI feedback, though teacher feedback may have carried over slightly better to the next task (Meyer et al., 2026). A review of 20 studies found a medium effect of automated writing feedback overall (Fleckenstein et al., 2023).
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets two cautions. Trained teachers still wrote better feedback than an AI in most categories when researchers compared them side by side (Steiss et al., 2024). Nearly half of students may ignore AI feedback entirely unless revision is required (Jansen et al., 2025). The grade stays with the teacher and never comes from the AI. The design that works, shown in Figure 2.6, makes revision part of the assignment and keeps the grade with the teacher.
